title: The Boy Who Swallowed a Star
summary: When a falling star lands in his field, Otto swallows it to keep his wish safe forever. The star lights him from within like a lantern — but a star was never meant to be kept, and to hold it is to slowly burn away, unless he can bear to give his wish to the sky.

chapters.title: The Star in the Field
chapters.body:
Otto was ten years old, and he had exactly one wish, and he had been saving it.

Everyone in the village of Dunmere knew you could wish on a falling star — but falling stars were rare, and most people, when they finally saw one, wasted the wish on something small, blurted out before they'd thought it through. A better pair of boots. A sunny market day. Otto had watched his whole village fritter away their falling stars on nothing, and he had decided, with the fierce seriousness of a ten-year-old, that when his star came, he would not waste it. He would save it. He had a wish worth saving — a big one, a real one, the wish that his father, who had gone away over the mountains to find work and not come back, would come home. Otto was saving his star for that.

And one autumn night, a star fell into his field.

He was lying in the barley at the edge of the farm, watching the sky as he did most clear nights, when one of the stars came loose from the black and streaked down — bigger and brighter and closer than any he'd seen, so close he heard it, a high singing sound — and it struck the earth at the far end of the field with a soft thump and a wash of gold light.

Otto ran to it. And there, in a small crater in the barley, lay the star. It was not large — about the size of an apple — and it was not hot, though it glowed a warm brilliant gold, pulsing gently like something breathing, or a heart. It was the most beautiful thing Otto had ever seen. And it was his. His star, his wish, come at last.

He reached to make his wish — to say the words, bring your father home — and then he stopped, seized by a sudden terrible worry. What if he said it wrong? What if he wasted it, the way the others wasted theirs, blurting it out too fast? This was his one wish, his only chance to bring his father home, and it felt too enormous, too important, to spend in a single careless moment. He wanted to be sure. He wanted to save it, to hold it, to keep it perfectly safe until the exact right moment when he was certain he'd get the words exactly right.

But a star, he could see, was already beginning to fade. Its gold pulse was slowing. Left in the field, it would burn out by morning, and his wish with it. He couldn't leave it. And he couldn't bear to spend it yet. So Otto did a foolish, desperate thing, the kind of thing a frightened child does when he wants to keep something too much: he picked up the warm glowing star, and — before he could think better of it — he swallowed it whole, to keep it safe inside him until he was ready.

It went down easily, warm and singing, and settled somewhere behind his ribs. And at once Otto felt it — a gentle golden warmth spreading through him, and a light, a real light, glowing out through his skin, faint gold, so that he stood in the dark field softly shining like a lantern.

He had done it. He had saved his wish. It was safe inside him now, and he could hold it as long as he liked, until the perfect moment came. Otto walked home through the dark, glowing softly, terribly pleased with his own cleverness, certain he had outwitted the falling star's one flaw.

He did not yet know that a star is not a thing you can keep.

chapters.title: The Light That Burned
chapters.body:
For the first few days, the swallowed star was wonderful.

Otto glowed. Faintly in daylight, brightly in the dark — a soft warm gold shining out through his skin, so that he needed no candle at night and cast a little pool of light wherever he went. The village marveled. Children followed him around. And Otto carried his wish inside him, safe and warm, waiting for the perfect moment to spend it, savoring the having of it.

But by the end of the first week, he began to notice that something was wrong.

He was always warm now — too warm. The gentle heat of the first night had grown, and grown, until it was a constant low burning behind his ribs, an ember that never cooled. He grew thirsty in a way water couldn't fix. He grew tired. And the light — the beautiful gold light — was getting brighter, not dimmer, as if the star inside him were flaring up, feeding on something. Feeding, Otto slowly realized with a cold fear, on him.

He went to the oldest woman in Dunmere, who knew the old things, and he confessed what he'd done — swallowed a falling star to save his wish. And the old woman's face filled with alarm.

"Oh, child," she said. "You mustn't keep a star. A star isn't a thing that can be held. Do you know what a star is? It's a wish already burning — burning to be spent, to be given, to be set free. That's what falling stars are: wishes flying to earth to be wished, and then to burn out, having been given away. That's the whole life of a star. It falls, it grants a wish, and in the giving it burns itself out — gladly, completely, the way a candle gives its light by spending itself. That's not the star's flaw, child. That's its whole purpose. A star is made to be given away."

Otto's stomach turned. "But I saved it. I kept it. So I wouldn't waste my wish."

"And now it's trapped," the old woman said gently. "A star that isn't spent doesn't stop burning. It can't. Burning is all it knows. You've swallowed a fire that's meant to be given away — and since you won't give it away, it has nothing to burn but you. It will keep flaring brighter, and burning hotter, feeding on you, until —" She stopped, and didn't finish, but Otto understood. Until there was nothing of him left. The star would consume him from the inside, glowing ever brighter, because he had tried to keep for himself a thing that only lives by being given away.

"Then I have to make my wish," Otto said, frightened. "Now. I have to spend it before it burns me up. I'll wish my father home, and the star will burn out, and —"

But here the old woman looked at him with a deep and difficult pity, because she knew the last hard part, the part Otto hadn't understood yet.

"You can spend it, child," she said. "But not the way you're thinking. A wish spent to keep something for yourself — to fill your own emptiness — that's not giving the star away. That's just another kind of keeping. The star can only truly burn out, and truly grant its wish, if you give it away freely — send it back to the sky, let it go, wish not for what you want to hold onto, but let the light go out of you and up and out into the world. And that means —" she said it as gently as she could — "you may have to give up holding on so tightly to bringing your father home. Not stop loving him. But stop clutching. The star won't free you while you're using it to clutch."

chapters.title: The Wish Given to the Sky
chapters.body:
Otto walked out into the field that night — the same field where the star had fallen — burning and bright, the gold light blazing out of him now so fiercely it hurt, lighting up the barley all around like noon. He was running out of time. The star was consuming him. He could feel it.

And he understood, at last, the terrible choice the old woman had laid before him. He had swallowed the star to keep his wish safe — the wish to bring his father home. He had held it so tightly, for so long, because letting go of the wish felt like letting go of his father. But the star could not be spent while he clutched it. To free the star — to let it burn out the way it was meant to, granting its wish and returning to the sky — he had to give it away freely. Not clutch it. Not use it to fill his own aching emptiness. He had to let the light go out of him and up and out, freely, for its own sake.

And that meant loosening his grip on the one thing he'd been holding onto hardest.

Otto stood in the blazing field and thought about his father. And he realized that he had turned his love for his father into a fist — a tight, desperate, clutching thing, a wish he gripped so hard it had started to burn him alive. He had thought that holding on tighter was how you loved someone who was gone. But the star was teaching him otherwise. The star only gave its light by letting go of it. And maybe — maybe love was the same. Maybe you didn't keep someone by clutching. Maybe you kept them by loving them with an open hand.

So Otto made his wish. But not the wish he'd been saving. He didn't wish his father home — didn't try to use the star to fill the hole, to clutch, to keep. Instead, standing in the field with the light blazing out of him, he opened his hands to the sky, and he let go. He wished, freely, for the thing you wish when you love someone with an open hand: not bring him back to me, but let him be well, wherever he is. Let him be happy. Let him be safe. And let me be all right, whether he comes home or not. He gave the wish away — gave it to his father, gave it to the sky, asked for nothing to hold onto, only for good to go out into the world.

And the star answered.

The light poured up out of Otto — all at once, a great gold column rising from his chest into the black sky, blazing, singing, free at last. It did not hurt. It was the opposite of hurting. It was like setting down a weight he'd carried so long he'd forgotten it was heavy. The burning behind his ribs cooled and eased and lifted, and the gold light streamed up and up, out of him and into the night, and burst high above into a scatter of new small stars that spread across the black and settled among the others, shining.

The star had burned out the only way it could — by being given away. And Otto stood in the dark field, emptied of the light, cool and whole and himself again, and he did not glow anymore, and he was not burning anymore, and he felt, strangely, lighter and freer than he had in all the long months since his father went away.

His father did not come home that night. This story will not pretend he did — the star had not been spent to clutch, and a wish given with an open hand does not always bring back what it lets go of. But something had changed in Otto. The tight, burning, desperate fist of his love had opened. He still missed his father, still hoped he'd return. But he no longer clutched it, no longer let it burn him from the inside, no longer held on so hard it hurt to live. He loved his father now with an open hand — hoping him well, wherever he was, and living his own life in the meantime instead of burning up waiting.

And whether because of the wish, or only because of the boy Otto had become, his father did come home — the following spring, over the mountains, thinner and older and overjoyed. And Otto ran to him with open arms, having learned the thing the star had taught him: that you do not keep what you love by swallowing it and holding on until it burns you. You keep it by loving it freely, with open hands, and letting the light go where light is meant to go — up, and out, and into the world.
